summary: Ryan 2012 (21818642), a 744-patient double-blind RCT, found that a ginger-root extract (0.5-1.5 g root equivalent/day) added to 5-HT3 antagonist plus dexamethasone reduced acute Day-1 chemotherapy nausea (primary, p=0.003), with no clear effect on delayed nausea, vomiting or quality of life. Viljoen 2014 (24642205), 12 RCTs and 1278 pregnant women, found improved nausea versus placebo (MD 1.20, from 2 trials, low quality) but no significant effect on vomiting. Both nausea contexts are credited only for those conditions; Dr. Pham's rejection of digestive/joint/inflammation/longevity transfer is encoded as excluded claims. 31937153 is abstract-only (dose not verifiable) and gets no context.

applicability.studied_population: Adult cancer patients on 5-HT3 antagonist plus dexamethasone chemotherapy antiemesis, or pregnant women with nausea and vomiting of pregnancy.

population.description: 744 adult cancer patients randomized in 23 community oncology practices (URCC CCOP) receiving chemotherapy with 5-HT3 antagonist plus dexamethasone on Day 1; 576 evaluable (91% female, mean age 53).

study_contexts.study_design: Phase II/III multicenter randomized double-blind placebo-controlled four-arm trial (placebo, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5 g ginger root equivalent/day); intent-to-treat mixed-model analysis.

outcomes.name: Acute nausea severity on Day 1 of chemotherapy (average and maximum, 7-point scale), all ginger doses vs placebo across cycles 2-3: significant reduction (p=0.013 average, p=0.003 maximum); largest with 0.5 g and 1.0 g/day
Delayed (Days 2-3) and follow-up (Day 4) nausea: significance weakened; vomiting and FACIT-G quality of life: no significant differences

limitations: Adjunct to standard 5-HT3 antagonist plus dexamethasone antiemesis; not stand-alone antiemetic efficacy, delayed-nausea benefit or general digestive benefit.

Dose values are ginger-root equivalents (each capsule 8.5 mg combined gingerols/zingerone/shogaol, equivalent to 250 mg root, in olive oil); not extract mass or interchangeable with other preparations. No dose-response: 1.5 g was not better than 0.5-1.0 g.
Chemotherapy emetogenicity and baseline nausea severity were not controlled (Discussion); 744 randomized, 576 analysed.
Returned decision A070: general digestive, joint, inflammation and longevity transfer rejected; this context is limited to acute chemotherapy-associated nausea.
Dr. Pham's fourth ruling set (2026-10-28): credit only for the studied nausea context; no digestive, joint, inflammation or longevity transfer.
Context authored and source-verified by agent review (Claude) on 2026-10-28; Dr. Pham's pre-approval of fully source-verified contexts attested by Sean on 2026-10-28.

dose.administration_frequency: Three capsules (or placebo) twice daily for 6 days, starting 3 days before chemotherapy, in study cycles 2 and 3.
dosage_forms: oral capsule (purified liquid ginger-root extract in extra virgin olive oil)
co_therapies: 5-HT3 receptor antagonist antiemetic plus dexamethasone on Day 1 of every chemotherapy cycle; ginger pulses tied to chemotherapy cycles 2 and 3.
dose.reported_regimen: Placebo, 0.5 g, 1.0 g or 1.5 g ginger-root equivalent per day as capsules of 250 mg root equivalent taken twice daily for 6 days starting 3 days before chemotherapy, cycles 2 and 3.

normalization.basis: Arm daily doses in ginger-root equivalent as reported by the source (250 mg root equivalent per capsule); not a universal threshold.

identity.chemical_form: Orally administered Zingiber officinale (powder capsules, extract or essence capsules, syrup, biscuits) in trial-specific preparations

population.description: Pregnant women with nausea and vomiting of pregnancy at any stage; 12 RCTs, 1278 participants (seven placebo-controlled; others vitamin B6, dimenhydrinate or metoclopramide comparators).

study_contexts.study_design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs of oral ginger for NVP (PROSPERO CRD42011001237); primary objective effectiveness on NVP; separate analyses by comparator.

outcomes.name: Nausea symptoms (change in VAS) vs placebo: MD 1.20 (95% CI 0.56-1.84), p=0.0002, I2 0%; pooled from 2 of 7 placebo trials
Number of vomiting episodes vs placebo: MD 0.72 (95% CI -0.03 to 1.46), p=0.06, I2 71%
Nausea vs vitamin B6: no significant difference

limitations: Pooled placebo nausea estimate rests on only 2 studies; most trials high risk of bias, variable outcome reporting and low-quality evidence (Abstract; Conclusions).
Doses 600-2500 mg ginger/day for 3-21 days, most 1000 mg/day powder for 4 days (Table 1; Discussion); dose subgroups are exploratory and do not set a threshold.

Short-term treatment of NVP only; spontaneous abortion RR 3.14 (0.65-15.11) vs placebo was not significant but rests on 2 studies; not a pregnancy safety determination, which stays with the safety owner.
Returned decision A070: general digestive, joint, inflammation and longevity transfer rejected; this context is limited to nausea of pregnancy.

Included-study PMIDs are taken from the source reference list (PMC BioC reference identifiers) for the 12 Table 1 trials; Basirat 2009 has no printed PubMed identifier and none is invented. These are membership pointers, not independent approvals.
